slides.title: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; it should fund the software business to profitability and keep quick commerce as a gated option

paragraphs.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; it should fund the software business to profitability and keep quick commerce as a gated option

Answer: no. Quick commerce is a growing market without a profit pool. Launching would lose money on every order at every level of performance anyone has observed, breach the board's 12-month runway rule within the first year, and turn the grocers who buy our software into competitors. The software business can reach cash break-even inside current cash.
Launching would lose money
We cannot afford it
Software is the better use of the cash
•  Market GMV grows ~42% a year ($1.8B → $5.1B, 2022–25), but both scaled incumbents lose $1.90–$3.40 per order; QuickBasket closed 4 of 11 cities
•  At benchmark-median inputs an order loses $2.67 before site costs and $6.17 after
•  The plan's +$2.02 per order needs all four levers above the best site ever observed; our own pop-up lost ~$12.60 per order
•  Pop-up customers do not repay their $38 acquisition cost at benchmark economics
→ pages 4–9
•  The plan needs $9.5M of our $12.0M cash to month 18; no new round is expected
•  It breaks the ≥12-month runway rule by month ~1 (if on top of today's $0.4M/month burn) or ~11 (most favourable reading)
•  At benchmark economics nine mature sites would lose ~$18M a year, 1.5× our total cash
→ page 10
•  Indicative model: cash break-even in ~26 months at today's 60% growth, cash never below $5.4M
•  Still works at 40% growth (break-even ~month 36); below ~30% costs must be cut
•  9 late-stage deals = $0.86M ARR; pipeline grocers want their own fast delivery from stores, so we sell them the tools rather than compete
→ pages 11–12
Decisions requested:  (1) decline the Parcelbird Now launch and its $5.4M capex;  (2) approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires;  (3) adopt the quarterly re-entry triggers on page 13.
Source: Board briefing pack (Tables 1–3, sections 7–10); Parcelbird analysis. Detailed calculations on pages 4–12 and in the appendix.

paragraphs.text: 1  IT WOULD LOSE MONEY  ·  MARKET
Quick-commerce demand is growing ~42% a year, but the scaled incumbents lose money on every order and one is already retreating
US quick-commerce grocery GMV, $ billions
Incumbent operators, 2025
Year-on-year:

What this tells the board
•  Scale has not fixed the economics: a national operator with $1.2B of revenue still loses $1.90 on each order before any overhead.
•  The regional model is worse and shrinking: QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%) in 2025.
•  "Nobody owns the Midwest" is more plausibly a sign of poor economics in mid-size cities than of an open prize.
•  Growth is therefore necessary but not sufficient; the question is whether Parcelbird can earn money per order (next pages).
(5.1 ÷ 1.8)^(1/3) − 1 = 41.5%. The founders' "over 40% a year" is confirmed.
Source: Board briefing pack, Tables 1–2 and section 5. Growth rates, CAGR and EBITDA margins are Parcelbird calculations.

slides.title: Our own Columbus pop-up performed below the benchmark median on every lever and lost about $12.60 on each order

paragraphs.text: 1  IT WOULD LOSE MONEY  ·  COLUMBUS POP-UP TEST
Our own Columbus pop-up performed below the benchmark median on every lever and lost about $12.60 on each order
What the test does and does not show
•  Fair caveat: a temporary six-week site is early on the density curve, and orders were still growing 18% a week (≈180 a day in week 1 to ≈410 in week 6).
•  But volume only spreads fixed cost. The −$6.21 lost before site costs comes from a small basket, heavy promotions and slow riders, which density alone does not cure.
•  Growth was bought: promotions at 12% of AOV and first-order credits. Without them the 18% weekly growth cannot be assumed to persist.
Implication for the right-to-win test
•  Running other grocers' dark stores did not translate into running our own better: the pop-up underperformed the 14 customer sites our software already serves.

Months for a retained customer to repay $173 of acquisition cost
Stated intent overstates real use
•  Survey: 44% of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery "at least weekly".
•  Behaviour: 22% of acquired customers were still ordering in month three, at 3.1 orders a month, below once a week (4.3).

•  The bases differ, but the direction is clear: the group still ordering is half the survey's 44%, and even it orders less than weekly. The survey also sampled only 25–39-year-olds, likely the keenest users.
Calc: plan $3.77 × 3.1 orders = $11.68 a month; $173 ÷ $11.68 ≈ 15 months after month 3, i.e. ≈ 18 months from acquisition, even on the founders' inputs.
Source: Board briefing pack, sections 6–8. Payback ignores orders by churned customers in months 1–2 and any churn after month 3; the two partly offset. Parcelbird analysis.

paragraphs.text: Why not a smaller test?

A single permanent site answers the wrong question: density is the uncertainty least able to rescue the economics (page 7), and the pop-up plus 14 customer sites already show where the levers sit. At ≈$2.6M it would take the lowest runway to ≈10 months even if software grows at 60%.

Source: Board briefing pack; Parcelbird analysis. Option B assumes one permanent site at benchmark-median economics for 12 months ($1.15M fixed cost, $0.6M capex), run alongside option C's software plan.

slides.title: We ask the board to decline the launch, fund four software hires, and revisit quick commerce only when measurable triggers are met

paragraphs.text: RECOMMENDATION AND NEXT STEPS
We ask the board to decline the launch, fund four software hires, and revisit quick commerce only when measurable triggers are met
Decide today (January 2027)
Next 90 days
Revisit quick commerce only if all hold
1.  Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; commit no dark-store capex.
2.  Approve ≈$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires.
3.  Adopt a cash guardrail: ≥12 months runway reviewed monthly, with a cost plan ready if trailing growth falls below 40%.
1.  Close the 9 late-stage deals ($0.86M ARR).
2.  Scope store-based fast-delivery tools (picking, batching, rider dispatch) with pipeline grocers that want to launch.
3.  Turn the pop-up's lessons (promotions, rider productivity) into product features for customers.
4.  Build a quarterly benchmark from the 14+ customer sites to track the triggers.
1.  A customer site sustains positive site-level profit for two quarters (today the best combination is −$1.76 per order).
2.  Rider minimum-pay rules in the target cities are settled and costed.
3.  The software business is cash-flow positive, or committed funding keeps ≥12 months runway after the launch budget.

Why this is low-regret:  declining now keeps the $12.0M, the grocer relationships and the data. Our software already sees the economics of 14+ fast-delivery sites every quarter, so we will know if and when the triggers are met without funding the experiment ourselves; a dark store can still be opened later for about $0.6M of capex.
Source: Parcelbird analysis. Trigger thresholds derived from pages 5–12.

paragraphs.text: Key assumptions behind the numbers
•  Benchmark medians from 14 customer sites represent what a new Parcelbird site would achieve; the delivery fee is already net of payment cost.
•  The plan's $9.5M is spread evenly over 18 months; runway is measured as cash ÷ current monthly burn.
•  Software costs stay at today's implied level (≈$8.1M a year excluding cost of goods) plus $0.8M of hires; ARR converts to revenue at 81% gross margin.
Source: Board briefing pack, sections 4, 10 and 11; Parcelbird analysis.

slides.title: Appendix 2: the runway, pop-up and software-path figures rest on simple calculations from the pack's numbers

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
Appendix 2: the runway, pop-up and software-path figures rest on simple calculations from the pack's numbers
Runway under the plan (page 10)
•  Reading A: burn = $0.40M + $9.5M ÷ 18 = $0.928M a month. 12-month floor = $11.1M, reached after (12.0 − 11.1) ÷ 0.928 ≈ 0.9 months. Cash = 0 after 12.0 ÷ 0.928 ≈ 12.9 months.
•  Reading B: burn = $0.528M a month. Floor = $6.3M, reached after (12.0 − 6.3) ÷ 0.528 ≈ 10.7 months. Month 18 cash = $2.5M = 6.2 months at the $0.4M software burn.
Pop-up ramp (page 8)
•  Six weeks at 18% weekly growth summing to 11,800: week 1 = 11,800 × 0.18 ÷ (1.18^6 − 1) ≈ 1,250 orders (≈180 a day); week 6 = 1,250 × 1.18^5 ≈ 2,860 (≈410 a day).
•  Loss ≈ 11,800 × −$12.57 ≈ −$148k (annualised fixed cost applied per order).
Software path (pages 11–12)
•  Today's total costs ≈ $4.1M revenue + $4.8M annual burn = $8.9M, of which cost of goods 19% × $4.1M = $0.78M and operating costs $8.12M; plus $0.8M hires = $8.92M.
•  Monthly ARR growth = (1 + annual growth)^(1/12); monthly burn = ($8.92M − 81% × ARR) ÷ 12. Break-even ARR = 8.92 ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M.
•  Results: 60% → break-even month 26, low point $5.4M, minimum runway ≈24 months; 40% → month 36, $2.7M, ≈18 months; 30% → rule breached ≈ month 23.
•  Option B adds $0.6M capex at month 0 and $2.03M of site loss over months 1–12: minimum runway ≈10 months at 60% growth.
Source: Board briefing pack, sections 1, 7, 8, 9 and 10; Parcelbird analysis.
